data.title: Tarmo Peltokoski begins HK Phil tenure with Mahler’s monumental Symphony No 8
data.description:
Gustav Mahler’s rarely performed Symphony No 8, a work requiring such a large orchestra and choir it is known as “Symphony of a Thousand”, finally received its Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra premiere on Saturday, heralding an ambitious new chapter as the 26-year-old Finnish conductor Tarmo Peltokoski officially took the podium as music director.
The 5pm performance at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre involved nearly 600 musicians and singers from six choirs: the Hong Kong Philharmonic Chorus; the Learners Chorus; the London Philharmonic Choir; St Paul’s Co-educational College Senior Mixed-Voice Choir; Ying Wa College Choir; and the Hong Kong Children’s Choir.
The monumental 85-minute piece, with performers pushing the stage to the limit and the choir occupying about a third of the seats on the balcony, formalised the start of the youthful maestro’s four-year contract as the ensemble’s ninth music director.
Peltokoski, the youngest music director in the HK Phil’s history, formally succeeded Dutch maestro Jaap van Zweden, who concluded a record 12-year tenure in 2024.
Mentored by the celebrated Finnish pedagogue Jorma Panula, the conductor arrived in the post having already performed regularly with the orchestra in the past couple of years to critical acclaim. Recently, a live Deutsche Grammophon recording of a one-hour arrangement of Richard Wagner’s “Ring” Cycle was also released.

Following the final bows inside the packed Hong Kong Cultural Centre Concert Hall, the celebration moved upstairs for a surprise reception on the fourth floor, organised by Bernhard Fleischer, who assumed the role of the orchestra’s chief executive on September 1 last year.
Peltokoski was led into the reception at around 7.30pm and was momentarily thrown by a slide show of images from his hometown, Vaasa, before he was swept up by VIPs demanding selfies.
Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui arrived just before 8pm to join musicians, HK Phil board members and guests. Peltokoski’s best friend, Samuel Eriksson, and his father Raine Peltokoski also joined the party.
David Cogman, director of Swire Pacific and chairman of the HK Phil, noted: “Tarmo said that the Mahler 8 is a work that should be reserved for very special occasions and tonight certainly qualifies.”
“When we started our search for a new music director, many of you will recall, our priority was to find someone who could build on the orchestra’s achievements, but also take it to a new artistic direction,” Cogman said.
“We had absolutely no idea what new direction might mean at that point. From the very first time when Tarmo worked with the orchestra, you could see the potential for all of this.
“The musicians responded to his deep understanding of the music, his artistic vision and above all, his energy. Tonight’s performance has given us a tremendously exciting vision of what we can achieve together in the years to come.”
Patrick Ren Xiaolong, deputy chief executive of the HK Phil, wrote Chinese calligraphy on site with the words for “welcome” as a gift to the maestro.
Law called the performance a splendid fanfare for the new era under Peltokoski’s baton.
“Great artistic synergy takes time to build, yet today it felt entirely natural. I’m fully confident that this strong partnership will elevate the Hong Kong Phil to new heights and enrich Hong Kong’s vibrant cultural scene,” she said.
“The Hong Kong government proudly supports the Hong Kong Phil in its further efforts to solidify its role as a cultural flagship of our city. Together, we will project Hong Kong’s artistic brilliance on the global stage, reinforcing our position as an East meets West cultural exchange centre.
“As a music lover myself, please allow me to express my warmest thanks to Tarmo and all the musicians for an unforgettable orchestral feast. Here’s to a new era for the Hong Kong Phil, one filled abundantly with breathtaking music, rewarding projects and exciting milestones ahead.”
The Hong Kong Gaudeamus Dunhuang Ensemble performed excerpts from Western opera using Chinese instruments at the reception.

Raine Peltokoski said he never thought his son would end up leading a Hong Kong orchestra. “I have been here four or five times now. My wife and I take turns to see him conduct here. We are very proud and we have learned so much about music through witnessing his progress.”
Under his contract, Peltokoski, who is also music director of Orchestre national du Capitole de Toulouse, principal guest conductor of the Rotterdam Philharmonic and principal guest conductor of the Deutsche Kammer­philharmonie Bremen, is scheduled to conduct in Hong Kong for seven weeks during his first full season.
Unlike his predecessor, who made a deliberate point of not socialising with orchestra members, Peltokoski has spoken of his wish to forge close personal connections with the players to counter the isolation that often accompanies life on the international conducting circuit.
From November 23 to December 6, he will take the orchestra on a European tour that will include a stop in Helsinki, Finland, his home country.

data.title: Canadian plan to clear Hongkonger migration backlog hailed but questions remain
data.description:
A Canadian goal of clearing a backlog of more than 30,000 applications from Hongkongers awaiting permanent residency is “encouraging” but questions remain about whether it can be achieved by 2027, advocates and immigration experts have said.
Experts and Canadian parliamentarians said on Saturday that Ottawa’s new one-off measure to add more quota spaces to clear the Hong Kong immigration pathways backlog would help address the uncertainty facing tens of thousands from the city still waiting for permanent residency.
Canada’s 2027-29 immigration levels plan, announced on Thursday alongside the budget, introduced a “time-limited measure” to allocate up to 100,000 additional spaces for permanent residency for specific humanitarian groups, including those under the Hong Kong pathways.
The government said the move, which would be in addition to the 380,000 permanent residence places for each of the next three years, aimed to “process all remaining applications” under the Hong Kong pathways by the end of 2027.
More than 48,500 Hongkongers applied under the bespoke scheme, which Ottawa launched in 2021 in response to the implementation of the national security law, before it closed to new applicants earlier this year.
But high demand and limited admission space have left tens of thousands in limbo, with wait times stretching as long as a decade.

In a letter shared online by Canadian parliamentarian Michael Ma, Canada’s immigration minister said that more than 14,500 permanent resident applications had been processed under the bespoke scheme since its launch.
“My department will fully honour our 2021 commitment and finalise all remaining applications under the Hong Kong pathways,” Lena Metlege Diab, minister for immigration, refugees and citizenship, wrote.
“This exceptional measure will provide space for up to 32,000 additional permanent resident admissions for Hongkongers, over and above the targets set out in the plan.”
The Hong Kong Pathway Alliance, an advocacy group that has been lobbying parliamentarians to introduce a one-off measure for Hongkongers, welcomed the move.
“The Hong Kong Pathway Alliance welcomes the government’s intention to address this long-standing issue and introduce new measures to help reduce the backlog,” it said in a statement shared online.
“We sincerely hope that all Hongkongers awaiting permanent residency will soon receive their PR status and be able to build stable, fulfilling lives in their new home in Canada.”
Willis Fu Yiu-wai, a senior immigration consultant with Goldmax Associates, described the announcement as a “positive development” that would give applicants greater confidence about their long-term status in Canada.
“One of the biggest challenges over the past few years has been the uncertainty,” he said.
“Many applicants have already settled in Canada, built their careers and families there, but are still waiting for a final decision on their permanent residence applications.
“The additional PR spaces are encouraging because they show that the government is actively looking at ways to address the backlog.”
But whether the backlog could be cleared by the end of 2027 was hard to predict as processing times depended on many factors, including background checks, document verification and the “complexity of individual cases”, he said
“Personally, I would be more confident saying that the backlog can be significantly reduced over the next one to two years, rather than saying it will necessarily reach zero by a specific date.”
Chak Au, a member of parliament with the opposition Conservative Party, said the measures were “welcome news” for many applicants who had faced years of uncertainty, but noted that few details were available yet.
“Applicants still need clear information about eligibility, processing timelines and how the quota will work,” he said in a social media post on Saturday.
“The announcement is an encouraging step, but it must be followed by timely and effective action.”
Jenny Kwan, a parliamentarian from the left-wing New Democratic Party who launched a petition in August demanding action on the issue, said her party would closely monitor how the measures were implemented.
“A policy promise is only as good as its execution,” she said.

data.title: China’s AI models, led by Kimi, rule open-source enterprise spending
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence models led by Moonshot AI’s Kimi family accounted for nearly nine-tenths of estimated global enterprise spending on open-source systems, according to a new study, even though proprietary US rivals continue to capture the vast majority of overall revenue.
The report, released this week by Silicon Valley venture capital firm Menlo Ventures, said Chinese AI systems accounted for 89 per cent of global enterprise spending on open-source models. Kimi led with a 61 per cent share, followed by DeepSeek at 15 per cent and Z.ai’s GLM series at 11 per cent.
By contrast, Meta Platforms’ Llama series, the leading Western offering in the category, accounted for just 7 per cent of open-source enterprise spending.
The global numbers were extrapolated from a September survey of nearly 400 US enterprise decision-makers managing more than US$4 billion in total AI budgets, alongside public filings and third-party reports, according to Menlo.
Unlike closed systems, open-weight models allow developers to download and adapt the underlying parameters rather than access them exclusively via hosted cloud services. Menlo groups such open-weight architectures under the broad label of “open-source”.
Despite the growing adoption of open Chinese architectures, proprietary systems still captured an overwhelming majority of model budgets.
US firms Anthropic and OpenAI commanded a combined 86 per cent of enterprise spending on AI models that were accessed via application programming interfaces (APIs), capturing 55 per cent and 31 per cent respectively, while Google held 9 per cent, the report showed.
In contrast, open-source models represented just 4 per cent of expenditure, even though they accounted for 19 per cent of enterprise usage of tokens – the processing units of AI data.
On global AI model aggregation platform OpenRouter, Chinese models’ token usage exceeded that of US models for the 27th consecutive week from October 26 to November 1.
The dynamic underscores an emerging division across the global AI supply chain: US giants lead in monetising closed-source APIs, while Chinese open models serve as foundations upon which overseas developers adapt to build their own services.
One example is US-based AI coding platform Cursor. In a technical report published in March, Cursor disclosed that its Composer 2 model was built on Moonshot’s Kimi K2.5. The US company refined the Chinese model on code-heavy data sets before applying reinforcement learning to improve its performance in software engineering.
In the report, Menlo said that coding tools and enterprise chatbots now made up 76 per cent of the US$77.3 billion global enterprise AI application market, with autonomous agents driving the next phase of business demand.
Menlo is an active investor in Anthropic, as well as several AI infrastructure providers examined in the report.

data.title: MTR Corp orders halt to unauthorised work at station after column concerns
data.description:
Hong Kong’s rail giant, the MTR Corporation, has ordered a contractor to fix substandard columns erected on the platform of a station under construction after discovering unauthorised remedial works to fill gaps of up to 30cm to the ceiling.
The corporation said on Saturday that routine inspections last month uncovered the incomplete works and that it had immediately instructed the main contractor, Bouygues-Dragages Joint Venture, to suspend the remedial works.
“During routine inspections of incomplete works in October 2026, we found that remedial works involving the filling of patching materials had been carried out at the heads of columns at the platform level of the Tung Chung West station construction site without the MTR’s prior approval,” a spokesman said.
“The MTR immediately instructed the main contractor to suspend the works concerned and launched an investigation to assess the condition of columns across the different zones at the station’s platform and concourse levels, as well as the associated work procedures.
“The identified issue does not affect the safety of the completed structure.”

The incident is the latest in a string of construction scandals that have plagued the city in recent months, from faulty lift installations to missing reinforcement bars at a luxury development and substandard concrete at a public housing estate.
The pervasive issues have intensified scrutiny of industry practices and exposed gaps in government oversight.
The spokesman said the main contractor was required to submit a comprehensive report on the matter and a proposed rectification plan. Work would resume only after the MTR Corp had approved the plan, alongside other necessary approvals, he said.
The corporation stressed that all remedial work would be carried out in full compliance with all statutory requirements before final acceptance of the works and that the main contractor would bear all related costs.
“The MTR Corporation attaches great importance to the supervision and quality of construction works on our railway projects, with robust assurance mechanisms and processes in place to ensure the quality of the works,” the spokesman said.
He added that relevant government departments had been told about the matter.
Photos obtained by media outlets showed four columns, of which two appeared to have gaps of about 20cm to 30cm between their tops and the roof due to missing concrete, with exposed steel reinforcement bars.
The South China Morning Post has approached the Buildings Department, Highways Department and the main contractor for comment.
In August last year, the MTR Corp received complaints after a media report alleged that a subcontractor working on Tung Chung East station had used tiles manufactured in mainland China rather than the German-made ones required under the contract.
It later filed a police report after it failed to resolve concerns about the authenticity of materials and documentation supplied by the subcontractor.
The MTR Corp confirmed that the materials were bricks used for partitions in station equipment rooms and that the main contractor later promised not to use that batch.
Edward Chan Sai-cheong, past chairman of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers’ Structural Division, said leaving a gap between the concrete and the roof was common in top-down construction.
He said the method involved erecting steel columns during foundation works, which allowed work on two levels at the same time and that the gap around the columns would be grouted later to fill it.
But he pointed out that the method should be approved in advance, adding that he had no insider knowledge of the MTR project.
“Generally, it should be stated clearly at the stage of approving building plans. It should not happen all of a sudden,” he said.
“In general, as long as the steel columns are properly grouted with appropriate materials, load transfer will not be affected.”
He added that the gap should be filled in any case, as a column should reach the roof.
Chan said the MTR had adopted a strict monitoring system on its projects, but there was still room for improvement.
He also said a new documentation requirement proposed by the Buildings Department could improve monitoring at construction sites, especially for concealed works.
Following the faulty steel reinforcement found at One Stanley, a luxury estate, the department proposed requiring all sites to keep photo or video records of steel reinforcement before concrete is poured. It plans to introduce the requirement by the end of this year.

data.title: Ex-husband’s DNA found on hammer allegedly used to kill Abby Choi: prosecution
data.description:
Warning: graphic content follows.
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung could have been fatally struck with a hammer that contained her ex-husband’s DNA when it was seized from a rural village flat where her dismembered remains were found, a court has heard.
Wrapping up their case as the murder trial entered its sixth week, prosecutors highlighted forensic findings and surveillance camera footage showing the movements of Choi and three of her former in-laws before and after her alleged murder on February 21, 2023.
Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, have denied conspiring to kill the influencer over what prosecutors depicted as a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat in Ho Man Tin.
The Kwong brothers admitted to preventing the lawful burial of the 28-year-old’s body before the trial began in late September. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also pleaded guilty to the charge midway through the trial.
Prosecutors allege that Kwong Kau, the registered owner of a luxury home at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate, enlisted his two sons to help kill his former daughter-in-law after she had tried to sell the flat she initially bought for her two children with Alex Kwong.

Choi’s ex-husband allegedly struck her on the head with a hammer during a car ride, when they were both in the back seat and ostensibly on their way to pick up their eight-year-old daughter from school on February 21, 2023, with Anthony Kwong driving the vehicle.
Part of Choi’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, was discovered in a 600 square foot rental flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei village three days later.
Forensic pathologist Dr Kwok Ka-ki, who conducted an autopsy on February 26 that year, said Choi could have died from severe brain damage or suffocation caused by blood blocking her airway after being hit on the head with a blunt object.
The autopsy report highlighted seven external injuries inflicted on Choi’s head before her death, including a 15cm (6-inch) laceration and a 5.5cm-by-5cm depressed fracture.
Asked whether the model’s head injuries could have been inflicted by a one-pound ball-peen hammer seized from the flat, Kwok said the injuries were consistent with those caused by the alleged murder weapon.
Defence counsel Trevor Beel, representing Anthony Kwong, suggested the injuries could have been caused by someone banging Choi’s head against a handle inside the car driven by the defendant.
Kwok acknowledged that possibility, but said it was more likely that the injuries had been caused by multiple blows to the head rather than a single impact against a stationary object.
Government chemist Wai Wing-kong, who conducted a DNA examination on the hammer, said he found Alex Kwong’s DNA attached to its handle, but the DNA found on its head was insufficient for analysis.
Wai said there was a one-in-6.2-billion chance for the DNA sequence in question to originate from a random person other than the defendant.

Alex Kwong’s lawyer Andrew Raffell suggested his client could have left his DNA on the hammer for innocent reasons, such as a drop of sweat on the handle. Wai said this was unlikely, unless a substantial amount of sweat came into contact with the surface.
Surveillance camera footage played in court allegedly showed the three defendants covertly transporting Choi’s body into the flat shortly after 3pm on February 21.
The Kwongs allegedly parked two Toyota Alphard seven-seater cars side by side and nose to tail outside the premises so that the body could be taken out through the narrow gap between the two vehicles.
Anthony Kwong, who was seen wearing a black T-shirt and black shorts, allegedly asked his younger brother to block the view of potential bystanders while he and his father moved a plastic box containing Choi’s body into the flat.
Anthony Kwong also allegedly spoke on the phone with his mother, Jenny Li Sui-heung, telling her to pick up Choi’s daughter immediately from school.
An anxious Li appeared to urge her younger son to leave the Kadooria flat in the early hours of February 22, the morning after the alleged murder.
“Quickly! The next step is coming now. Oh my god. I’m very afraid. Just go!” the mother, who is not a defendant in the present trial, was heard saying in CCTV footage retrieved from the luxury home.

That day, Alex Kwong took a taxi to West Kowloon and arrived at a high-rise rental flat at The Arch, the court heard. Prosecutors previously alleged that Kwong Kau had asked a friend, Wu Zhirong, to rent the flat to be used as his younger son’s hideout.
Anthony Kwong and his father were seen leaving and returning to the village flat in Tai Po multiple times between February 21 and February 23.
Surveillance cameras also captured the elder Kwong buying three saws from a hardware store in Sham Shui Po on February 23.
The last video played in court showed Alex Kwong leaving the West Kowloon residence at 4.32pm on February 24. He was arrested at Tung Chung Development Ferry Pier shortly after 1pm the next day.
The defence is expected to begin presenting evidence before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and the nine-member jury when the trial resumes on Monday.

data.title: Why wealth managers see opportunity in Hong Kong despite Beijing’s tax crackdown
data.description:
Global financial leaders who gathered in Hong Kong this week largely sidestepped Beijing’s offshore trust tax crackdown, a lingering near-term hurdle for the city’s otherwise expanding wealth management industry.
Beijing’s move earlier this year to step up scrutiny of wealthy families’ overseas assets was barely discussed openly at a series of financial industry events, including the Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit and the PWMA Wealth Management Industry Summit 2026, even as it remains a thorny issue for cross-border wealth management.
Industry heavyweights instead focused on the city’s appeal as an alternative safe haven amid global market volatility and its growing strength as a cross-border wealth hub.
Hong Kong had seen “continued momentum” in wealth management, helped by a record year for assets under management and a surge in net inflows, according to a report released on Thursday by the Private Wealth Management Association (PWMA) and KPMG China. The survey covered most of the association’s 44 institutional members.
Total private wealth assets under management in Hong Kong reached HK$12.9 trillion (US$1.65 trillion), up 24 per cent from a year earlier and “comfortably surpassing” the previous peak of HK$11.3 trillion in 2020.
The sector, however, faced a more complex operating environment amid geopolitical tensions and an evolving cross-border tax and regulatory landscape, the report said.
“Greater tax transparency” and “more rigorous reporting requirements” were increasing the complexity of cross-border wealth arrangements in the short term, the report said, citing respondents.
China’s Ministry of Finance said in July that the country’s 20 per cent personal income tax rate applied to investment gains from offshore trusts, raising concerns about Hong Kong’s role as a wealth destination for affluent mainland Chinese investors.
As evolving cross-border tax regimes in Europe forced wealthy families to “step up their game”, awareness was also “growing substantially” in Asia, said Marc-Andre Sola, founder and chairman of financial services and insurance brokerage firm 1291 Group, during a panel discussion at the PWMA summit on Thursday.
Chinese regulators were taking steps to ensure clarity on taxation by defining what worked from a tax point of view and what did not work, meaning structures that had been used did not work any more and leaving “a lot of room to restructure”, he said.
Still, experts have previously argued that clearer offshore trust taxation rules that eliminate grey-area practices would enhance the long-term credibility of Hong Kong’s trust industry.
Greater tax transparency could “strengthen confidence in Hong Kong over time”, according to the PWMA report.

data.title: ‘Hypocritical’: Hong Kong hits back at criticism of Joshua Wong’s sentence
data.description:
Hong Kong has hit back at a joint statement from 10 countries over the latest sentencing of opposition activist Joshua Wong Chi-fung, accusing them of distorting facts and smearing the city’s national security law.
The rebuttal came after the US, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the UK issued a joint statement on Friday saying the sentencing of Wong, together with the earlier jailing of many others, showed how the city’s national security law (NSL) was being used to “target individuals for political expression and participation”.
Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison for his role in a global campaign to instigate sanctions against mainland China and Hong Kong in the wake of the 2019 anti-government protests.
“We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the NSL and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to uphold their international commitments and honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British Joint Declaration [1984],” the joint statement said.
A government spokesman said on Saturday that the joint statement disregarded facts, blatantly interfered with the exercise of judicial power and maliciously slandered the national security law.
“The government strongly urges the relevant countries to immediately cease interfering in Hong Kong affairs, which are purely China’s internal affairs,” he said in a statement.

The spokesman reiterated that Wong had pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces, and that Hong Kong courts had strictly followed legal provisions and judicial procedures, “handing down the sentence independently and impartially based on objective facts and sufficient evidence, fully embodying Hong Kong’s spirit of the rule of law”.
“The government urges the relevant countries to stop making irresponsible and misleading remarks, and to cease interfering in any manner with the operation of judicial proceedings in the city and with Hong Kong affairs, which are internal affairs of China,” he added.
“Any attempt to undermine the government’s resolve to safeguard national security is doomed to fail and will never succeed.”
The spokesman also said the “groundless attacks” by the countries had exposed their “hypocritical double standards”.
“There are numerous cases in the countries concerned where their own citizens as well as foreign nationals have been prosecuted on charges such as ‘foreign agent’ and ‘foreign interference’, not to mention instances of arbitrary arrest and malicious prosecution,” he said.
Wong, 30, had been due to complete a sentence of four years and eight months for conspiracy to commit subversion on January 7 next year.
The High Court ruled on Thursday that he and fugitive former lawmaker Nathan Law Kwun-chung had partly contributed to sanctions and other adverse measures against mainland and Hong Kong officials, significantly undermining national security.
The court ordered the two months and two days remaining on Wong’s earlier national security sentence to run concurrently with his new jail term, pushing his expected release date back to November 2036.
The joint statement noted that the 10-year term came after “a further charge” under the security law and that many others had been jailed under the law before him.
In a separate case, three former leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China – the group behind the city’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil – were sentenced to up to seven years and three months for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.
They were former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan, former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung and former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan.

data.title: Hong Kong paediatrician urges parents to vaccinate children as temperatures fall
data.description:
A Hong Kong paediatric expert has called on parents to arrange influenza vaccinations for their children ahead of cooler temperatures next week, warning of a double whammy of overlapping summer and winter flu seasons.
The city has recorded 29 cases of severe paediatric influenza infection this flu season, two of which were fatal.
Dr Mike Kwan Yat-wah, former president of the Asian Society for Paediatric Infectious Diseases, warned on Saturday that the city could see a longer flu season with the winter and summer waves overlapping.
“Cold weather makes it easier for viruses to spread, mainly because lower temperatures toughen up the envelope, and the respiratory droplet particles are finer and smaller in dry weather. They can travel farther and can remain suspended in the air for a longer period,” he said in a radio interview.
“Meanwhile, many different kinds of viruses are active in winter, apart from influenza, such as the respiratory syncytial virus and Covid-19 … if one contracts different kinds of viruses at the same time, the condition is more serious and may require a longer hospitalisation.”
Temperatures are expected to drop to as low as 18 degrees Celsius (64.4 Fahrenheit) on Tuesday as a cold front hits the city early next week.
Kwan said children and the elderly could develop severe symptoms such as low blood pressure or inflammation in multiple organs after catching the flu due to a “cytokine storm”.
“When our body comes into contact with these pathogens, it triggers an immune response. When such a response is excessively intense, it can suddenly trigger an inflammation of multiple organs, causing the condition to rapidly deteriorate,” he said.
Kwan said a vaccine would lower the risk of a cytokine storm by introducing a very low dose of antigens under controlled conditions to stimulate the body to generate an immune response. As a result, when people encounter this pathogen again, their bodies can mount a very rapid and appropriate immune response to control the disease, he said.
Kwan also called on residents to improve their personal hygiene, such as washing their hands before touching their eyes, nose and mouth, and to refrain from going to work or school when feeling unwell and to see a doctor immediately.
“Many parents thought a stomach ache was caused by gastrointestinal problems, but a stomach ache along with constant nausea would be a symptom of myocarditis,” he said.
If residents caught the flu and were prescribed Tamiflu – an antiviral medication to treat influenza – they must finish the whole prescription, even when the symptoms had improved, Kwan said.
He added that a second-generation antiviral drug only required one dose, which could help patients with lower drug compliance or caring difficulty.
According to the Centre for Health Protection, as of October 25, only 27.5 per cent of children aged six months to five years, 36.4 per cent of children aged six to 11 and 26.7 per cent of children aged 12 to 17 had received seasonal influenza vaccination through government vaccination programmes.

data.title: Tiger Brokers targets Hong Kong growth as Beijing curbs overseas stock trading
data.description:
Tiger Brokers is seeking to offset the effects of Beijing’s regulatory crackdown by tapping business opportunities in Hong Kong, according to its CFO.
“User growth is currently mainly driven by local Hong Kong clients, and overall client growth remains very strong,” said John Zeng, Group CFO and CEO of Tiger Brokers (Hong Kong), when asked about Beijing’s scrutiny of unauthorised cross-border stock trading.
“We will certainly fully comply with regulatory requirements in acquiring new clients.”
Tiger Brokers, one of the region’s largest online brokerages and backed by Chinese smartphone maker Xiaomi, reported quarterly and nine-month records for new funded accounts in Hong Kong, Zeng said. The nine-month total exceeded the full-year figure for 2025, he added.
Retail client assets in Hong Kong nearly doubled year on year in the three months to September and rose more than 40 per cent from the previous quarter. The average first deposit by Hong Kong users was about US$30,000, the highest among the group’s licensed markets, Zeng said.
“We therefore firmly believe Hong Kong has huge growth potential, and we are confident that our quality products and services will attract and serve more local investors,” he added.
On May 22, the China Securities Regulatory Commission moved to penalise Tiger Brokers, Futu Securities International and Longbridge Securities for giving mainland Chinese investors access to overseas stocks without licences.
Tiger Brokers was ordered to pay 410 million yuan (US$61 million) in fines, and its illegal gains were confiscated. Mainland accounts have been barred from making new purchases or deposits since June 12.
UP Fintech Holding, the parent of Tiger Brokers, announced early this year that it would invest US$100 million in Hong Kong over one to two years. Zeng said the firm could increase that figure if growth momentum continued, though no specific figure had been set and “adjustments will be made dynamically”.
But acquiring other brokerages remained unlikely, he added.
The group is also expanding its local wealth management team. Its headcount in Hong Kong had doubled in just over a year, far outpacing its original two-year target, Zeng said.

data.title: Test of trust for Hong Kong’s new housing checks unit after Wang Fuk Court blaze
data.description:
For former Wang Fuk Court resident Dorz Cheung, seeing will be believing when it comes to reforms initiated after the deadly inferno in Hong Kong’s Tai Po district.
The 34-year-old questioned whether the new oversight bodies would prevent another disaster, saying systemic reforms to tackle shoddy building maintenance and bid-rigging could be undermined by poor implementation.
“No matter how well the system is reformed, it is people who put it into practice. Even the best system will achieve nothing if officials fail to enforce it or take responsibility,” Cheung said.
Industry observers said the new body overseeing public housing maintenance should make its operations transparent and align enforcement practices to restore public confidence after the Wang Fuk Court blaze, which claimed 168 lives last November.
The calls came after concerns were raised that the reform was “old wine in a new bottle”, particularly as the new body – the Public Housing Building Control Section (PBC) – retained some staff and practices of its predecessor, the disgraced Independent Checking Unit.




The independent committee investigating the Wang Fuk Court fire identified the unit, which oversaw public rental and subsidised-sale estates sold or divested by the Housing Authority, as the government department most responsible for the blaze, Hong Kong’s deadliest in decades.
Carmen Lai, chairwoman of the building surveying division of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, said improving transparency was crucial for rebuilding public confidence.
“Not until the fire did the public have an idea about which estates fell under the purview of the Independent Checking Unit. The public should have ways to learn about the new section’s duties and estates under its control,” she said.
“The section can also consider providing a regular update on the estates under maintenance, such as the progress on their application, approval and works, so the public can obtain more information and improve transparency.”
The unit was established in 2000 after a series of scandals concerning short piling that led to the demolition of two public housing blocks.
As of June, it oversaw 333 public rental and subsidised-sale estates, their retail facilities and car parks.
Under the reform, the new section will be set up this month, operating under the Housing Bureau and reporting to the permanent secretary for housing.
The PBC will also be audited by the Buildings Department, the principal authority on building works control. The committee criticised the department for failing to conduct a proper audit of the Independent Checking Unit.

Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun earlier defended the reform. He said the committee had not recommended changing the framework and that maintaining the current structure “still makes considerable sense today”.
Wong added that the PBC would adopt a fresh project-based approach to regulating maintenance works at individual estates, step up communication with the department and train the retained staff members, who were more familiar than other civil servants with the details of public housing estates.
Poor coordination between the Independent Checking Unit and the department in enforcing building work control was one of six problems, alongside the unit’s enforcement failures and deficiencies in the design of regulation, that the independent committee identified across both entities.
For example, the unit had only become aware of a site safety inspection policy nearly 2½ years after it was adopted by the department. That was despite regular meetings between the two departments, senior professional officers being seconded from the Buildings Department to the unit and semi-annual progress reports submitted from the unit.
The unit also notified professionals and contractors before inspection, whereas the Buildings Department made surprise checks. The committee said working attitude seemed to be the “only explanation” for this divergence, given the numerous communication channels between the two departments.
Lai said that although the Buildings Department would second a directorate officer to the new section to improve coordination, enforcement practices between the two departments still needed to be aligned.
“It can only make a change when the two departments have conducted reviews, reorganised their workflow and eliminated grey areas of administrative procedures and enforcement,” she said.
Lai also stressed the importance of staff training, saying this should cover new operational details, knowledge of building laws and the mindset of managing safety risks.
Her suggestions responded to the independent committee saying the unit had a “slack working attitude”, failed to properly investigate complaints and did not carry out its regulatory duties.
Lai added that the PBC should assess projects and inspect sites proactively, rather than rely on document reviews.
According to the Housing Bureau, since last December the unit had stepped up inspections of major maintenance works at buildings under its purview, covering 29 blocks across five public housing estates.
A veteran professional in the building maintenance industry, who was familiar with how the government operated, said the PBC could set internal key performance indicators to track its performance and gradually make targets publicly available after smoothing out its operations.
The insider added that retaining staff from the Independent Checking Unit, who were familiar with the design and plans of public housing estates, could help the operation of the PBC.
The source added that the directorate officer seconded by the department would have a key role in providing technical directions and striking a balance between rigorous safety compliance and avoiding excessive delays or increasing repair costs.
The insider also said the reform was timely, as the unit only started supervising large-scale maintenance projects in the past decade, when public housing estates were ordered to undergo inspections and repairs under the mandatory inspection scheme for buildings at least 30 years old.
“Only more public housing estates will age beyond 30 and require renovation … The workload will be heavy. The reform has provided direction for sorting out the arrangements and reallocating resources.”
As of 2025, about 29 per cent of the 1,722 buildings regulated by the unit were aged at least 40, and another 37 per cent were aged between 30 and 39, according to statistics compiled by the Legislative Council.

Daniel Lam Chun, a surveyor and former non-executive director of the Urban Renewal Authority, the city’s statutory body on the redevelopment and rehabilitation of buildings, also urged authorities to use the reform to build a sustainable framework for property maintenance as Hong Kong’s building stock continued to age rapidly.
He suggested that officials and officers should be regularly trained to eliminate risks at building works and the administration could explore using new technology to strengthen supervision.
Lam added that it was also important to educate property owners about their civic duties, such as maintaining their properties and monitoring the performance of professionals, contractors and government departments.
“The reform should not only treat the symptom but also the cause.”

data.title: Domestic helper arrested after allegedly spitting into 4-year-old girl’s food
data.description:
A foreign domestic helper in Hong Kong has been arrested on suspicion of ill-treating a child after she allegedly spat into the food of a girl under her care, according to police.
The mother of the four-year-old girl filed a police report at 9.28am on Friday, saying her 37-year-old Filipino helper had treated her daughter inappropriately.
Initial police investigations at the family’s flat at The Belcher’s, a private residential estate in Kennedy Town, indicated that the helper had spat into the victim’s food.
The helper is being held by police, and the case remains under investigation. The girl showed no visible injuries and did not require hospital treatment.

data.title: HKUST president Nancy Ip wins Unesco prize for Alzheimer’s research
data.description:
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) president Nancy Ip Yuk-yu has been awarded a United Nations prize for her “outstanding contributions” in neuroscience, which have enabled the earlier diagnosis and better monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease.
Ip was presented with the Unesco-Equatorial Guinea International Prize for Research in the Life Sciences on Friday in Paris.
“Dr Nancy Yuk-yu Ip, president of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, is a world-renowned neuroscientist recognised for her outstanding contributions to neuroscience, which have advanced understanding of brain function and Alzheimer’s disease,” Unesco said in a statement.
It added that her research had led to the discovery of new biomarkers, the identification of genetic risk factors and the development of blood tests that enable earlier diagnosis and better monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease. She has also conducted pioneering research in gene therapy for neurodegenerative diseases.
“Many scientific breakthroughs are the result of cooperation, particularly interdisciplinary cooperation. I believe we should further strengthen cooperation across disciplines, universities and national borders,” Xinhua quoted Ip as saying.
“This will play an important role in developing medicines for diseases such as Alzheimer’s. We are currently working towards this goal.”
Ip is also a member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
The other two laureates are Professor Carlos Martin Montanes of the University of Zaragoza in Spain and Professor Adnane Remmal of Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University of Fez, Morocco. They were honoured for their major contributions to the development of a live attenuated vaccine against tuberculosis and the fight against antimicrobial resistance, respectively.
Established in 2008 by Unesco and funded by the Republic of Equatorial Guinea, the Unesco-Equatorial Guinea International Prize for Research in the Life Sciences aims to recognise individuals and institutions that have made outstanding contributions to improving the quality of human life through research in the life sciences, while promoting progress in the field and the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

data.title: Hong Kong draws growing interest from Irish firms seeking expansion across Asia
data.description:
More Irish companies are considering Hong Kong as a base for expansion across Asia, according to the head of the country’s chamber of commerce in the city, who described the two as “natural partners”.
Padraig Seif, president of the Irish Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said momentum was building ahead of the Asia-Pacific Irish Business Forum as Irish firms increasingly looked to Asia amid Washington’s tariff policy and the lingering effects of Brexit.
“What we’ve seen is … Asia and Hong Kong in particular were really a hard sell previously. People were not interested,” Seif told the South China Morning Post in an exclusive interview ahead of the forum.
“I believe that it’s perfect timing for Irish businesses being more open for this area of the world, for this area of the world looking for business opportunities into Europe and taking a look at Ireland for that, but also providing opportunities for regional Irish businesses to do more business with Hong Kong.”
The two-day forum, which begins on November 19, coincides with the city’s hosting of the Asian Gaelic Games. It is expected to draw about 200 attendees from across the region for discussions covering sectors including finance, aviation and pharmaceuticals.
Government representatives from Ireland and Hong Kong are also expected to attend, with Ireland’s ambassador to China, Nicholas O’Brien, set to deliver opening remarks.
Seif said the forum would serve an “educational” purpose alongside promoting business and trade between the two jurisdictions.
He added that many people in Asia remained unaware that Ireland had become a leading hub for technology giants, medical science companies and financial services.
“It’s not only a green field with cows on it,” he said. “The vast majority of exports from Ireland to this part of the world are electronics and pharmaceuticals and optical products, high-value items.”
Seif described Hong Kong and Ireland as “natural partners”, citing their shared use of English, common law systems and low-tax policies.
“If you’re coming from Hong Kong, Ireland is ‘plug-and-play’,” he said, referring to a device or software that works as soon as it is connected.
Ireland’s commercial presence in Hong Kong remains relatively limited compared with that of its Western peers. Many of the country’s biggest companies, including the Bank of Ireland, have no presence in the city.
But there are signs of change.

Seif said the chamber’s individual membership had risen from 30 to 123 over the past three years, while corporate membership had grown from three to 14.
Immigration Department figures showed that 1,715 Irish nationals were living in Hong Kong in September, up 25 per cent from the end of 2025, nine months earlier.
A source familiar with the Irish business community said about 35 businesses were active across the Greater Bay Area, which comprises Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in Guangdong province.
The source added that many Irish firms that previously had offices in Hong Kong left during a wider corporate exodus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. But emerging opportunities in mainland China and attractive commercial rents were drawing their attention back to the city.
“They are all considering redeploying to Hong Kong,” the source said.
Among the forum’s speakers is Irish entrepreneur Patrick Malloney, who is establishing a Hong Kong presence for his health sciences company, P4ML.
The firm, which specialises in precision medicine and rare diseases, is part of a newborn screening consortium whose members include AstraZeneca subsidiary Alexion.
Malloney cited Hong Kong’s talent pool and its universities among his reasons for choosing the city, saying it had “some of the best universities to work with”.
Alongside establishing a base in Hong Kong, he is seeking Series A funding for the company and considering a potential initial public offering on the city’s stock exchange.
“This isn’t me just coming in to shake hands and look good. This is me coming in saying I can relocate to Hong Kong … and create jobs that bring value to the economy,” he said.
Specialist auditing firm Valaston also recently marked the official opening of its first Hong Kong office.
Founded in 2007, the firm focuses exclusively on the asset management industry and, as well as Ireland, has offices in the Netherlands, the Cayman Islands, Singapore and the UK.
Paul Kinsella, a partner at the firm, said growing interest in Hong Kong fund structures, together with recent tax and regulatory developments, had made the city an “increasingly attractive base” for asset managers.
“For a professional services firm like ourselves, the decision is built around where our clients are,” he said.
“We felt the time was right to move from servicing the market primarily from elsewhere to making a proper long-term commitment here.”

data.title: Call to end ‘unjust’ national security cases as Hong Kong slams ‘malicious attacks’
data.description:
Ten countries – including the “Five Eyes” allies – have called for an immediate end to “unjust prosecutions” under Hong Kong’s national security law after opposition activist Joshua Wong Chi-fung was jailed for 10 years, while the government has urged foreign forces to stop their “baseless malicious attacks”.
The foreign ministers of the 10 countries issued a joint statement on Friday, a day after the High Court sentenced Wong over his role in a global campaign to instigate sanctions against mainland China and the city following the 2019 anti-government protests.
“These are further examples of how the national security law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation,” said the statement from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.
“We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the national security law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to uphold their international commitments and honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British Joint Declaration in 1984.”
They also cited the case of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, the group behind the city’s annual Tiananmen Square vigils.
Three former leaders were sentenced to jail terms ranging from five years and two months to seven years and three months under the national security law.
Wong’s sentence earlier drew criticism from the European Union and the US. Beijing responded by pointing to Hong Kong’s efforts to safeguard national security and urging foreign countries to stop interfering in China’s internal affairs.
Earlier in the day, the Hong Kong government condemned what it called “smears and slanders” from “various countries led by the US and the West”, alongside other “anti-China media”, overseas organisations and politicians, saying their moves “precisely reflect that the interference and threats from external forces still exist”.
“[The government] will continue to resolutely fulfil its duties and obligations to safeguard national security, combat and pursue those anti-China and destabilising elements as well as agents of external forces, while simultaneously protecting the lawful rights and freedoms enjoyed by Hong Kong residents and others in Hong Kong in accordance with the law,” a government spokesman said.
The government urged them to “recognise the objective facts and stop making any baseless malicious attacks and interferences”, he added.
Wong, 30, earlier pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces. He had been scheduled to complete a sentence of four years and eight months for conspiracy to commit subversion on January 7 next year.
But the latest sentence means Wong’s expected release date has been pushed back to November 2036.
The Five Eyes intelligence alliance comprises the US, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

data.title: Hong Kong’s yacht industry eyes mainland China buyers but challenges remain
data.description:
Hong Kong’s yacht industry is seeking to attract more buyers and visitors from mainland China under a new cross-boundary travel scheme, but relatively high berthing costs could pose a challenge, industry representatives have said.
Industry leaders, exhibitors and visitors gathered in Discovery Bay on Friday for the fourth edition of the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show, which runs until Sunday.
The show featured more than 30 vessels, including superyachts and models from international brands such as Sunseeker, Princess and Azimut.
The Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme, which allows eligible Guangdong-registered yachts to sail into Hong Kong waters, was launched last month as part of Hong Kong’s broader efforts to develop its yacht economy.
Franklin Mak, executive vice-president of hospitality at HKR International, the developer behind the Lantau Yacht Club, said the yacht economy extended beyond vessel sales to include tourism, hospitality and related services.

Tommy Ho, chairman of the Hong Kong Yachting Association, estimated that mainland buyers could account for about 200 additional yacht purchases in Hong Kong under the new scheme, while local demand was expected to remain steady.
Ho said his organisation had recently received a growing number of inquiries from mainland yacht enthusiasts interested in visiting the city, including requests for sailing routes and tourist destinations.
Liao Kai, chairman of the Zhuhai Yacht Association, said the new arrangement was also expected to strengthen links between Hong Kong’s yacht services and Zhuhai, which was a major yacht production centre.
While Hong Kong could offer mainland buyers a wider choice of international brands and quality second-hand vessels, Liao said the city’s relatively higher prices of yachts compared with the mainland could make it less attractive.
Bryan Van Dale, an international yacht-equipment supplier, said the main downside of Hong Kong’s boat business was that moorings were too expensive and in short supply.

data.title: More funding could be sought if HK$10b university town loan scheme falls short
data.description:
Hong Kong’s education secretary has said she will seek additional funding if a HK$10 billion loan scheme falls short of the needs of institutions setting foot in the Northern Metropolis’ first university town, while warning that their financial plans must be feasible and they must not “take chances”.
A task force jointly established by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Hong Kong Association of Banks will designate 11 tertiary institutions as public sector entities to help them secure bank financing for projects in the Northern Metropolis.
Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin told a Legislative Council panel meeting on Friday that institutions seeking to establish themselves in the university towns, as well as lawmakers, had called for more financial support.
She also told some media outlets that she would seek additional funding from the financial secretary if institutions approved to set foot in the first university town needed more than the HK$10 billion earmarked for loans.
“In addition to the government loan, we will encourage and line up different government departments to form platforms to let institutions present their development proposals to some potential investors to secure flexible financing,” she told the education panel meeting.




The government plans to develop three self-financed university towns, with a core campus area totalling 300 hectares, in the Northern Metropolis megaproject near the border with mainland China, fostering collaboration among industry, academia and the research sector.
Three university towns are planned: the 26-hectare Hung Shui Kiu university town; the 100-hectare San Tin university town; and the 180-hectare Ta Kwu Ling university town. The government earmarked a HK$10 billion loan scheme for the first one, Hung Shui Kiu university town.
The Hung Shui Kiu town and its adjoining technology and industry areas will be developed as a “centre for applied post-secondary education in smart manufacturing and global talent cultivation”.
Institutions wishing to establish a presence in Hung Shui Kiu must submit their proposals by the end of next month, with the government expected to announce the successful bids early next year.
Choi said institutions had to secure funding from diverse sources, as existing rules stipulated that the government loans could not exceed 50 per cent of project costs. She warned that the institutions had to formulate a feasible financial plan to repay the loans.
She said the Designated Vetting Group, led by the chief secretary, would review the institutions’ proposals and assess their financing arrangements to see if they were feasible.
“We will not tolerate any situation where an institution suddenly finds itself unable to repay its debts. Therefore, institutions must not rely on wishful thinking or take chances during their planning,” she said.
At a meeting of Legco’s financial affairs panel, Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang, deputy chief executive of the Monetary Authority, said the Northern Metropolis Financial Advisory Taskforce, set up in April, would discuss ways to help universities secure loans from banks at its next meeting.
The task force was set up to explore financing solutions to support the development of the Northern Metropolis.
Yuen said the authority would list nine universities and two post-secondary colleges as public sector entities in its Banking (Capital) Rules.
“It will make it considerably easier for them to secure financing solutions when carrying out developments in the university towns,” he said.

Lawmaker Andrew Yao Cho-fai, council chairman of Lingnan University, welcomed the move and said his institution was preparing a proposal for the Hung Shui Kiu project.
“This is a very promising start … because our primary concern is funding. Aside from borrowing from the government, we hope to secure more financing from commercial banks,” he said.
The government previously said the Hung Shui Kiu university town had three plots, each with a maximum plot ratio of five.
The largest site covers 165,200 square metres and can yield 826,000 square metres of total floor space, with the plot to be handed over in stages from 2026 to 2029.
The second covers 52,800 square metres, with 264,000 square metres of floor space. The handover is scheduled between 2027 and 2029.
The smallest is 43,700 square metres, allowing 218,500 square metres of floor space under a 110-metre height limit, with the site handover scheduled for 2027.

data.title: Hong Kong firms must innovate to compete in mainland China, trade chief says
data.description:
Hong Kong companies can survive intense competition in mainland China by being innovative and maintaining high standards, the head of the city’s trade promotion body has said.
Hong Kong Trade Development Council chairman Frederick Ma Si-hang said on Friday that the city was also tapping into emerging markets in Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa to counter global trade uncertainties.
“I feel that Hong Kong manufacturers need to be more innovative; think of ways to use our strengths to penetrate this huge mainland consumer market,” he said.
“We need to know what their tastes are before we can penetrate this market.”
Ma was speaking on the sidelines of the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, which has attracted more than 400 Hong Kong exhibitors this year.
He said businesses should capitalise on Hong Kong’s unique advantages, including the “one country, two systems” governing principle. The city’s professional services providers could also use their expertise to help mainland companies expand globally.
He added that Hong Kong was exploring emerging markets to counter global trade uncertainties following the elections in the United States.
“We have seen that many emerging markets are actually giving Hong Kong a lot of momentum, and growth is relatively strong,” he said.
“While we must take care of our traditional markets on one hand, on the other hand, we are also exploring some emerging markets, such as Central Asia, the Middle East and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.”
Ma said the council would open an office in Egypt next year to expand its promotional network in Africa amid geopolitical shifts.

He added that Hong Kong was catching up fast in innovation and technology, which would allow closer cooperation with the mainland.
“The artificial intelligence trend will not stop, and there is a trend that China’s development might be faster than the United States,” he said.
Ma cited views that the US election results could slow the country’s technological progress while China continued to advance rapidly.
He also expressed hope that Hong Kong would overtake London in global financial centre rankings next year. He pointed to what he described as the city’s achievement in surpassing Switzerland in wealth management, saying this was “not simple”.
Standard Chartered’s CEO for Hong Kong, Greater China and North Asia, Mary Huen Wai-yee, said the Shanghai expo highlighted the Chinese market’s immense potential.
She added that the bank was helping businesses connect with the world as China continued to open its market.
“This year, Standard Chartered continues to act as a superconnector, showcasing innovative results in areas such as cross-border trade, wealth management and sustainable finance, using the power of finance to connect China and the world,” she said.
“The import expo allows the world to share the dividends of China’s development and also shows the huge potential of the Chinese market.”

data.title: Crypto heavyweight eyes Hong Kong expansion to tap growing tokenisation demand
data.description:
Solana, one of the world’s largest blockchain networks, plans to expand in Hong Kong to tap the city’s growing demand for tokenisation, according to a senior executive.
“I believe that the biggest opportunity for Solana is actually in [the Asia-Pacific region],” Solana Company chairman and CEO Joseph Chee said in an interview in Hong Kong earlier this week.
Founded in the US in 2018, the company is behind one of the most popular cryptocurrencies. With a market capitalisation of about US$53 billion on Friday, the Solana token was the world’s seventh-largest cryptocurrency, according to CoinMarketCap.
The Solana Foundation was established in 2020 to maintain the blockchain network bearing its name, while Nasdaq-listed Solana Company focused on “acquiring and holding” its tokens and “offering public market investors direct exposure to Solana”, according to a December filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
In Hong Kong, Solana Company had positioned itself as a digital asset infrastructure and service provider, the firm said last month after being named a “strategic enterprise” by the city government’s Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises.
The company said it planned to use its Hong Kong operation, which also serves as its new Asia-Pacific headquarters, to explore how digital asset infrastructure could “contribute to the city’s financial institutions”.

Hong Kong has identified tokenisation as a key area of fintech development, with a growing number of firms launching blockchain-based financial products.
Julia Leung Fung-yee, CEO of the Securities and Futures Commission, said at the annual Hong Kong FinTech Week earlier this week that regulators had authorised 17 tokenised retail products with total assets under management of US$1.3 billion, up 34 per cent from a year earlier.
Still, the US was “moving a lot faster” in tokenisation, Chee said.
“A lot of major financial institutions in Hong Kong are just starting to think about or initiate a [tokenisation] project,” he said, adding that the company expected to have “a good sense of where Hong Kong is” within about six months.
Solana Company aimed to grow its Hong Kong team to as many as 30 employees from fewer than 10 currently, according to Chee. If no major tokenisation service providers emerged in the city within the next six months, “we might just build a team” to meet demand from local banks, he said.

data.title: Hong Kong authorities arrest 28 in crackdown on bid-rigging after Tai Po fire
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities have cracked down on a bid-rigging syndicate and arrested 28 people, including directors of contractors and consultancy firms as well as some with triad backgrounds, in the first operation by a joint task force after the devastating Wang Fuk Court fire.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that the task force, formed to combat bid-rigging, had also set up a 24-hour hotline for the public to report any suspected bid-rigging activities and would offer monetary rewards in appropriate circumstances.
The arrests are the first since a damning report on the deadly Tai Po blaze by an independent committee was released last week.
Tang told a press conference that the government had taken action after discovering a triad-related bid-rigging group was pushing through deals before more measures came into effect.
“They hoped to ‘take the last bus’ and used excuses such as price fluctuations of materials, urgency to start the projects, to trick owners to quickly sign the contracts, and so they could choose the project consultants and contractors of the syndicate,” Tang said.
“They hoped to seek exorbitant profits at the last minute.”
Those arrested included managing directors and staff members from six contractors, 10 consultancy firms, one property management company and one owners’ corporation.
Some of them had triad backgrounds, Tang said.
He said the group had obtained 12 contracts for building projects across Hong Kong, involving about HK$100 million (US$12.7 million), using illegal means such as coercion, bribery and blackmail.
Senior officials from the Independent Commission Against Corruption and the Competition Commission also attended the press conference.
The joint task force – involving police, the Independent Commission Against Corruption and the Competition Commission – was set up to combat crimes related to bid-rigging in maintenance projects following the release of the committee’s report.
The housing estate was undergoing large-scale renovation works when the blaze broke out last November, killing 168 people.
The government also announced last week that it was set to criminalise bid-rigging in building maintenance projects under laws covering triad and corruption offences and allow authorities to take criminal or civil action against such conduct.
The change will introduce a criminal offence with penalties of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and fines.
According to the committee’s report, bid-rigging and associated misconduct may involve multiple parties such as building contractors, consultants, property management companies, middlemen, building management committee members and even homeowners, with some of them having triad affiliations.
The committee said that while it was not within its scope to determine whether there had been bid-rigging in the Wang Fuk Court case, there were “numerous features of that project which bore the hallmarks of bid-rigging and anti-competitive conduct”.
